page_title: Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests

summary.title: Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests
summary.one_liner: Google Testing Blog argues for keeping the testing pyramid weighted toward unit and integration tests, because slow, flaky end-to-end tests create long feedback loops, and the reader comments debate that position.
keywords: how many end-to-end tests should i write
takeaways: End-to-end tests simulate real user scenarios but bring disadvantages such as slowness, instability and a long feedback loop.
The testing pyramid suggests most tests should be unit tests, with fewer integration and end-to-end tests.
Commenters note that the right mix depends on the product, the team, and whether the system is legacy or new.
Commenters also suggest monitoring can complement tests, and that E2E tests can still catch cross-component bugs that unit tests miss.
summary.summary: This Google Testing Blog post by Mike Wacker argues against adding more end-to-end tests, citing their cost in time, instability and slow feedback, and recommends keeping the testing pyramid shape. The main body is short; most of the page is a long comment thread. Commenters push back on several points, including whether the advice fits legacy systems, CD environments, and agile teams, and whether E2E tests are still needed for integration bugs. The page does not give detailed metrics or code examples beyond a hypothetical scenario about a team losing days to a slow suite.
